moat.description: Global two-sided network in mobility and delivery with rider-driver liquidity that no rival can replicate at the same density — moat is real, autonomy is the existential question, and the Waymo relationship is the clearest crack since the June review.
moat.analysisSummary: Uber's moat is **network density across mobility and delivery in 70+ countries** — durable in the human-driven era, and still the default demand-aggregation layer into autonomy, though the partnership path is no longer one-sided:

analysisPoints.title: Liquidity Network Effects
analysisPoints.text: Uber's wait-times, surge dynamics, and supply density in major cities cannot be matched without simultaneous rider and driver acquisition at scale. Lyft, Bolt, and DiDi compete city-by-city; only Uber holds the global liquidity stack across both mobility and delivery. Q2 2026 added 208M MAPCs (+16% YoY) and 3.9B trips (+18% YoY) — more first-time users in the past twelve months than in any period over the past five years.

analysisPoints.title: Cross-App Bundling and Membership
analysisPoints.text: Uber One bundles mobility + delivery + grocery + ad-supported value, creating cross-category retention. Uber One reached 50M members in Q1 2026 and now drives roughly half of total Mobility and Delivery gross bookings. The July 2026 Delivery Hero takeover offer (€41.50/share, ~$14.8B equity value, close targeted H2 2027) would nearly double dual mobility+delivery markets from 34 to 58 and extend the bundle into Korea, MENA, LatAm, and foodpanda Asia — pending regulatory clearance and the SSW carve-out of 14 overlapping markets.

analysisPoints.title: Autonomous Demand Layer — Partnership Thesis Under Stress
analysisPoints.text: Uber still positions itself as the consumer demand and dispatch layer for autonomy (Rivian up to 50K R2 robotaxis from 2028, Wayve, NVIDIA 100k-vehicle network targeting 2027, 30+ AV partners, ~300K autonomous trips/week on the platform). Management committed $10B+ to scale the AV platform and targets 15 AV cities by year-end 2026. The flagship Waymo relationship has frayed: the Phoenix pilot ended at its contracted term in May 2026, and a July 2026 FT report said Waymo has told Uber it intends to enter Austin and Atlanta on its own from January 2028 when the current exclusivity allows — though management confirmed on the Q2 call that Waymo operations continue in Austin and Atlanta and that Uber is diversifying beyond any single partner. Wayve received Transport for London PHV licences in August 2026 with 100K+ riders signed up for London autonomous rides. Toyota fully exited its ~5.1M-share Uber stake in Q2 2026 (13F), ending the 2018 AV partnership investment — symbolic rather than operational, but a signal that legacy OEM capital is rotating away from the aggregator model. Tesla continues Cybercab production at Giga Texas and its own ride-hailing expansion in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, while Waymo delivers 500K+ paid robotaxi rides weekly on its own app. The demand-aggregator thesis is intact as a strategy; exclusivity with the leading US robotaxi operator is no longer the base case.

growth.description: Q2 2026 gross bookings $58.0B (+24% YoY, +22% cc) beat the ~$57.2B Street estimate; Mobility +22% (+20% cc), Delivery +26% (+25% cc). Adj EBITDA $2.8B (+33% YoY) at 4.9% of gross bookings; Non-GAAP EPS $0.81 (+35%) landed in line. Revenue $14.2B (+12% YoY) missed slightly as business-model changes shaved 8pp off reported growth. TTM free cash flow exceeded $10B for the first time. Q3 guide — gross bookings $58.25–$60.25B (+18–22% cc, midpoint ~$59.25B), adj EBITDA $2.86–$2.96B, EPS $0.84–$0.88 — trailed consensus on bookings and EPS, and the stock fell ~6% to ~$68. Organic bookings compounding remains strong; the market reaction reflects soft forward guidance and the revenue miss, not a bookings deceleration.

growthAnalysis.scoreDerivation: Base ~82 on a 17.5% midpoint of the 15–20% bookings CAGR — anchored to Q2's +22% constant-currency print and the guided 18–22% Q3 range, decayed for autonomy and Delivery Hero integration drag rather than extrapolated. +2.7 trajectory (Delivery and Uber One accelerating; Mobility stable at +20% cc for two quarters) +4 margin (adj EBITDA +33%, 4.9% of bookings) −10 high autonomy risk (Waymo own-app path dated to 2028 in Austin/Atlanta; Tesla Cybercab production continuing) = 78. Q3 guide slightly below Street is charged in the narrative, not the CAGR — the midpoint still sits inside the band.

growthAnalysis.keyRisk: Waymo has ended the Phoenix Uber pilot and, per a July 2026 FT report, has informed Uber it will enter Austin and Atlanta independently from January 2028; Tesla continues Cybercab volume production and its own consumer ride-hailing network in Texas metros. If Tesla scales direct-to-consumer demand aggregation or Waymo's own app displaces Uber on the densest US robotaxi routes, Uber loses pricing power on the highest-margin urban trips by 2028–29. Separately, the Delivery Hero offer (~$14.8B equity value, €14B bridge facility, close H2 2027) adds merger-control and leverage execution risk before any accretion lands.

valuation.description: At ~$68 (Aug 5 close; down ~6% post-earnings) Uber trades ~28% below the base case ($95) and ~36% below the ~$107 Wall Street average target (Strong Buy consensus, 32 analysts), at ~21× consensus FY26 EPS (~$3.30) and ~7% FCF yield on record TTM FCF exceeding $10B. The stock is down ~18% YTD and ~33% below the $101.99 52-week high despite Q2 bookings beating and adj EBITDA margin expanding to 4.9% — robotaxi competition (Waymo, Tesla) and a Q3 guide that trailed Street expectations remain the multiple compressors. The post-print selloff improves margin of safety without changing the autonomy overhang.

peAnalysis.summary: Uber remains a free-cash compounder with network durability trading at a fear-discounted multiple after the Q2 print. Bookings beat and TTM FCF crossed $10B, but revenue missed and Q3 EPS guidance trailed consensus — the market chose the forward guide over the organic beat. Since June the two structural facts are unchanged: Delivery Hero (optionality, H2 2027 close) and a clearer Waymo own-app path in Austin/Atlanta from 2028. The post-earnings pullback moves spot closer to the bear end of the scenario ladder without resolving the autonomy question.

learnedInterfaces.note: Consumer learning curve on rider app and habit formation is real but easily transferred.

businessLogic.note: Dispatch, surge, ETA prediction, and routing algorithms are differentiated but increasingly replicable by autonomy operators.

publicDataAccess.note: N/A — Uber is not a public-data access business.

talentScarcity.note: Marketplace engineering and operational scale talent is broadly available.

bundling.note: Uber One mobility + delivery + grocery + advertising bundle is genuinely differentiated; Delivery Hero would extend the dual-product footprint from 34 to 58 markets if the H2 2027 close lands — only DoorDash + Lyft attempt anything similar at much smaller scale today.

proprietaryData.note: Trip-level supply/demand data across 70+ countries is genuinely unique and feeds dispatch + pricing + autonomy partner integration.

regulatoryLockIn.note: Local rideshare licences, AV partnership integrations, and city-level relationships create switching friction in many markets.

networkEffects.note: Two-sided rider-driver liquidity in major cities is the textbook example of network effects; rivals struggle to replicate density without years of subsidy. Q2 added 208M MAPCs (+16%) and 3.9B trips (+18%). Autonomy operators with their own apps (Waymo, Tesla) are the structural test of whether that liquidity still compounds on Uber's surface.

transactionEmbedding.note: Stored payment, defaults, and travel/expense corporate integrations make Uber the default rideshare for both consumers and enterprises.

systemOfRecord.note: Uber is the system of record for mobility identity and history for ~150M+ active monthly riders globally.

tenMoats.verdict: Uber's network, bundling, and transaction-embedding moats remain AI-resilient — language models do not erode rider-driver liquidity. The Delivery Hero offer would deepen the bundling moat geographically if it clears. The AI-era structural threat is still autonomy: robotaxis (Waymo, Tesla Cybercab) attack the human-driven mobility network that anchors the moat. Since June that threat has become more specific — Waymo's Phoenix pilot ended, Austin/Atlanta exclusivity now has a dated end (own-app entry from January 2028), and Toyota exited its Uber stake in Q2 2026. Q2 earnings reinforced the organic side: record user acquisition, TTM FCF above $10B, and ~300K autonomous trips/week on the platform with 30+ partners — but management's $10B+ AV investment commitment and diversification beyond Waymo confirm the aggregator thesis is a bet, not a lock. Tesla vertical integration and Waymo's own-app expansion are the primary tail risks.
